props.title: Slightly Scarlet

sections.content: Slightly Scarlet stands as a fascinating noir-tinged Technicolor thriller that pushes against conventional crime film aesthetics. Director Allan Dwan, working with legendary cinematographer John Alton, created something unique - a color film with stark noir sensibilities. Like Leave Her to Heaven (1945) and Niagara (1953), it proves film noir's shadowy atmosphere could work brilliantly in color. The film follows two sisters - one a reformed criminal, one a kleptomaniac - caught in a web of political corruption and crime, starring John Payne, Arlene Dahl, and Rhonda Fleming.

sections.content: The film's most striking achievement is how it translates classic noir visual techniques into Technicolor. Cinematographer John Alton, famous for black-and-white noir masterpieces like T-Men (1947) and Raw Deal (1948), brings his signature style of dramatic shadows and canted angles but adds vivid reds and blues that create an almost hallucinatory effect. This approach influenced later color crime films like Point Blank (1967) and Chinatown (1974).

The psychological complexity of the sisters' relationship anticipates later explorations of duality in films like Vertigo (1958) and Single White Female (1992). The film's examination of political corruption and crime connects it to other noir political exposés like The Big Heat (1953) and Force of Evil (1948), though its Technicolor presentation gives these themes a uniquely garish quality. sections.content: Slightly Scarlet represents a crucial bridge between classic black-and-white noir and the more stylized color crime films of the 1960s and 70s. Its influence can be traced through Harper (1966) to neo-noir classics like Body Heat (1981). The film's bold use of color to enhance rather than diminish noir atmosphere proved that the genre could evolve beyond its monochrome origins.
